abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) is a promising approach for quantitative measurement in biology. Traditional lifetime measurements have limited photon throughput and slow acquisition speed due to photon counting electronics and point-scanning detectors. Wide-field imaging with optical gating can overcome these limitations. We analyze lifetime estimation precision for both single- and bi-exponential decays with optical gating waveforms. We focus on electro-optic (EO-FLIM) gating approaches that can be implemented all-optically with no photon loss and compare them to standard binning methods. Fisher information (FI) is used to calculate the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) for decay parameter estimation for each gating strategy, which is then verified with maximum likelihood estimation on Monte Carlo simulated data. We present fundamental limits for both single and bi-exponential estimation with resonant, step, and square gating waveforms. For single exponential decays, a single step or resonant gate approaches the FI limits from time correlated single photon counting (TC-SPC) within a factor of 1.2-1.6x. We map the parameter space for laser excitation waveform, gate waveform, and gate number. For bi-exponential estimation, at least 3 parallel step or resonant gates are required to estimate the full parameters. With prior knowledge of one lifetime, two optimally-chosen gates can approach the TC-SPC limit within 1.6x (step gate) or 2.9x (resonant gate). Estimation precision converges within 5-10 gates across conditions with one known lifetime component and within 10-15 gates with no prior information. Asymptotic performance with increasing gate number achieves between 3.1x (step) and 3.7x (resonant) the TC-SPC limit with one known lifetime and between 3.5x (step) and 8.8x (resonant) with no prior information. These results inform the design of sparse gating strategies that maximize throughput and per-photon information for lifetime estimation. Optical gating enables future experiments for high-throughput sensing and multiplexing of fluorescent biosensors without relying on time-resolved detector electronics.
